title: Hey Arnold! The Movie
full_review:
"Hey Arnold! The Movie" (Paramount) is another Nickelodeon cartoon television series to come to the big screen, but the humdrum comedy lacks the inventiveness to make it anything more than a 74-minute version of a TV episode.

The hero of the story is a feisty young boy named Arnold (voiced by Spencer Klein) whose football-shaped head and knobby ears are his distinguishing characteristics -- along with the fact that he eternally looks on the bright side. His dilapidated, multi-ethnic neighborhood is about to be torn down by a group of developers led by Mr. Scheck (voiced by Paul Sorvino, a wonderful choice), a heartless man who also happens to be a sharp dresser. Arnold is joined in his fight to save the neighborhood by his black friend Gerald (Jamil Smith), whose hair is piled high on his head a la Marge Simpson, and Helga (voiced by Francesca Marie Smith), a pigtailed girl who outwardly insults and hates Arnold, but is secretly stuck on him and so helps him surreptitiously. With their help, Arnold must find a document that proves that his six-square-block area is a national historical landmark.

Younger viewers are likely to be more amused by the film than their adult chaperones, chiefly because it shows kids single-handedly taking on the bad guy, while the adults mainly do nothing. The film also preaches about the evils of giant corporations (hey, aren't Nickelodeon and Paramount giant corporations?), while talking about the value of seeing the silver lining to every cloud. However, there are a few elements that are likely to go over the heads of younger audiences, but may trouble parents nonetheless. For example, Helga sneaks up to her attic to "pray" to a statue she has created in Arnold's image that is surrounded by lit candles.

The voice talent is refreshing, with Christopher Lloyd playing a creepy yet goofy city coroner and Jennifer Jason Leigh voicing a curvy "Charlie's Angel" spy with zillions of gadgets that she lends to Arnold. Director Tuck Tucker's film rarely rises to the witty heights it aims for as flat animation and a drawn-out story lack creativity. With the script skimming ideas off of several live-action blockbusters, from "Men In Black" to "Mission Impossible 2" and even films like "Scooby-Doo," the movie plays like an action film for kids.

The feature also has a slight dark side, which may intrigue a younger audience, and serves to balance out the saccharine moments. Older children may be fine with these elements as well as the cartoon explosions and mayhem; it's up to the parents' discretion.

Because of some cartoon violence and menacing scenes, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. 2002
